back: Enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions (exothermic).
Enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state; always endothermic.
Enthalpy change when each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms gains one electron to form gaseous 1− ions.

front: Why the second electron affinity is endothermic
back: The electron is added to a negative ion, which repels it, so energy must be supplied.

front: Lattice energy from a Born-Haber cycle
back: ΔHlatt = ΔHf − (atomisations + ionisation energies + electron affinities), each multiplied up for the formula.
Larger ionic charges and smaller ionic radii (higher charge density) give a more exothermic lattice energy.
½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g): half the Cl–Cl bond energy.
Double the anion terms (atomisation and electron affinity) and use IE₁ + IE₂ for the 2+ cation.

front: Why first electron affinity is less exothermic from Cl to I
back: Electron added further from the nucleus with more shielding, so it is attracted less strongly.
